_doc: THE MERGE QUEUE. The manager SCHEDULES merges; it does not resolve the
conflicts that not scheduling them causes.
⚠️ THIS FILE DID NOT EXIST UNTIL 2026-09-03, AND ITS ABSENCE IS THE POINT.
The day manager ran a merge queue that morning -- it declared an order, it
held sessions at position 2+, it promoted and poked -- and it worked. But it
existed only in that session's context. It was cited to a sub-session as
'the state of record ... created today', and a search of every branch and
every commit in the repo found NOTHING: not on main, not on any ref, not in
history. What existed was docs/runbooks/merge-queue.md, which is prose.
That is the exact failure the operator named on 2026-09-03: 'that's one of
the base functions of what a manager session is supposed to do. That needs
to be canonized. It's not something you take upon yourself in the session.'
A queue held in a session's head dies with that session, and the next
manager re-derives it from scratch -- or does not, and the morning repeats.
MEASURED HARM on the day the queue was invented, which is why it exists:
26 merges to main, 19 of them (73%) touching a shared register, five of
those the manager's own and two of THOSE bare lease heartbeats -- merges
whose entire content is a timestamp. Every one re-conflicted every open PR
touching a register. #10918 went dirty three times; #10923 the moment it
went green. Sessions burned ~16-minute pytest-runs that were void before
they finished.
THE INVARIANT THIS FILE EXISTS TO HOLD, and the one check_manager_scope.py
R8 enforces: AT MOST ONE ENTRY IS REBASING AT A TIME. Two sessions rebasing
against the same moving main is the thundering herd the queue prevents; it
is also the state that looks fine to each session individually, which is why
it needs a check rather than a convention.
PROMOTE AND POKE. A session does not poll. When position 1 lands, the
manager sets the next entry to `rebasing` AND messages that session. An
entry left `waiting` with nothing ahead of it is a session sitting idle for
a promotion nobody sent -- the 46-minute block the operator caught, in a
different costume.
STATES, NEVER COLLAPSED:
waiting   -- in the queue, not yet cleared to rebase. Do NOT rebase.
rebasing  -- cleared, and the ONLY entry that may be. At most one.
green     -- rebased, CI passed, waiting on the manager's merge click.
merged    -- landed. Keep the row until the next manager reads it.
blocked   -- cannot proceed; `blocked_on` says why. NOT `waiting`:
'not my turn' and 'cannot go' are different facts.
⚠️ `green` IS THE STATE THAT COST US. #10923 sat green and mergeable from
11:01:05Z to 11:11Z and the OPERATOR noticed before the mechanism did. The
manager's own 11:04Z sweep timer was enabled, carried next_run_at 11:04:00Z,
and never fired -- no error, no log. A cadence check that graded whether a
sweep was ARMED would have passed straight through that hole, because it WAS
armed. See check_manager_scope.py's R7 note for what is and is not covered.
note: STATE 2026-09-10T02:47Z. ONE entry `rebasing` (#11626) and that is the R8 invariant, not a coincidence — its owner is poked and cleared; nothing else may rebase until it lands. They were measured 2026-09-09T04:16Z and many have since merged or closed; this file has not been reconciled against a live open-PR list since. That is stated rather than silently carried, and it is deliberate: the census in this same file records that the queue GREW 30 -> 42 across a window in which ten PRs were merged, because every merge to main spawns a reconcile-open-prs — draining one at a time while still merging does not converge. A successor must NOT open a session on 'drain the queue'. What IS current in this file is the non-automation entries and tonight's ledger. ⚠️ AND DO NOT READ THE `blocked` COUNT AS A BACKLOG OF WORK — R13 blocks every bot-opened PR by construction (a bot writes no merge_slot claim), so `blocked` there is the steady state of a mechanism, not a queue of things waiting on a decision.

digest_clearance._what: How to clear digest-liveness when it is about to go `stale` and red every open PR. THIS CORRECTS THE PROCEDURE I CARRIED IN MY OWN WAKES FOR THREE HOURS, which named the wrong artifact and would have wasted the pass it was written for.
digest_clearance.⚠️_the_stuck_receipt_prs_CANNOT_clear_it: THE CARRIED PLAN SAID 'land the newest stuck work-digest PR'. THAT IS WRONG AND WOULD HAVE CLEARED NOTHING. check_digest_liveness grades the receipt on the MERGED TREE, so landing a receipt OLDER than the one main already carries advances last_digest_age by zero. Read per branch at 04:16Z, generated_at: #11442 2026-09-08T19:23:13Z · #11445 19:54:09Z · #11452 20:35:07Z · #11465 22:42:40Z · #11471 23:49:25Z. EVERY ONE IS OLDER than main's 00:58:39Z. They are dead weight on the queue, not a clearance path. ⚠️ AND THERE ARE FIVE, NOT FOUR — #11471 was absent from my own carried list, so the count I was managing to was wrong as well as the method.
digest_clearance.the_only_proven_clearance: DISPATCH-THEN-ARM, and it is proven exactly once end to end. At 00:57:49Z I dispatched work-digest.yml (run 34297202160); it opened #11477 on automation/work-digest-34297202160-1; I pushed a merge_slot claim naming THAT branch onto it (42d9251f — check_manager_scope graded it 'a LANDING act, not an item' under the R2 carve-out); it merged 01:04:29Z. Verified AFTER, against a fresh main rather than inferred from the merge: `digest-liveness: OK state=fresh last_digest_age=0.38h`.
digest_clearance.⚠️_timing_matters_a_dispatch_can_produce: Run 34298416713 (event=schedule, 2026-09-09T01:14:57Z) completed `success` and opened NO PR, because digest_due correctly said not-due against the then-fresh receipt. So a dispatch fired early yields nothing to arm and is not a way to bank clearance in advance. Fire it CLOSE to the window — ~06:50Z for this one.
digest_clearance.⚠️_not_a_new_finding_do_not_re_file: work-digest.yml declares `20 * * * *` and had no run at all between 01:14:57Z and 04:16Z (3.0h). That is OI-20260902-HOURLY-DIGEST-CARRIER-PREPARED-AND-HELD-FOR-A-TIER-2-OK, which already measures the carrier at 5 firings a day against 24 declared and holds the systemd-timer replacement on a Tier-2 operator OK. It is prior art, not a fresh observation, and re-filing it would be the accumulation this repo complains about.
digest_clearance.the_durable_fix_is_routed_not_taken: MI-208-WORK-DIGEST-ARMS-A-LANDING-ROUTE-IT-CANNOT-COMPLETE — work-digest.yml writes .github/pr-landing/automation-work-digest-*.json but never the merge_slot claim R13 requires beside it. That is a .github/workflows/ path, which check_manager_scope R2 bars the manager from authoring. It stays `ready` and unassigned. ⚠️ The sibling producers (error-feed-digest, reconcile-open-prs, session-reaper, data-commit, econ-calendar) arm the same route — 26 of the 30 entries here are automation — so establish the denominator before anyone fixes one file.
digest_clearance.⚠️_remeasured_0521Z_expect_to_dispatch_r: Re-measured 2026-09-09T05:21Z against the COMPLETE run history of work-digest.yml (total_count 347): the most recent run is still 34298416713, event=schedule, 2026-09-09T01:14:57Z — **4.1 HOURS AGO**, against a declared `20 * * * *`. At 04:16Z the same gap read 3.0h; it has simply kept growing, and no run has fired in between. ⚠️ THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THE 06:58:39Z WINDOW: do NOT plan on a scheduled run producing a fresh receipt in time. Treat DISPATCH as the expected path rather than the fallback — check for a newer run first, but expect the check to come back empty and budget for the dispatch. ⚠️ STILL NOT A NEW FINDING AND STILL NOT TO BE FILED: this is OI-20260902-HOURLY-DIGEST-CARRIER-PREPARED-AND-HELD-FOR-A-TIER-2-OK, which already measures the carrier at 5 firings a day against 24 declared and holds the systemd-timer replacement on an operator OK. What is recorded here is the OPERATIONAL consequence for the clearance procedure, not a re-observation of the defect.

closed_unmerged._what: PRs that left the queue WITHOUT merging. They are not `entries` because R8's state vocabulary (blocked | green | merged | rebasing | waiting) has no term for closed-unmerged — correctly, since a merge queue holds only what can still go. Recorded here rather than deleted: neither appears in OPEN-PRS.json, whose contract scopes it to PRs IN FLIGHT that the manager did not open, so this is the only register that carries them.
closed_unmerged.⚠️_i_invented_a_state_and_the_guard_caug: I first wrote these four rows as state `settled`, which is outside the closed vocabulary, and R8 failed the commit naming every row. The vocabulary exists so that 'not my turn' (waiting) and 'cannot go' (blocked) stay different facts; inventing a sixth value quietly widens it. Two of the four were genuinely `merged` and are back in entries with their merge commit cited.

⚠️_THIS_FILE_WAS_DEAD_FOR_SEVEN_DAYS_AND: MEASURED 2026-09-17T15:00Z. The 57 entries this file carried were written 2026-09-10T05:32Z by a DIFFERENT manager (session_01HrmZ1RRNM4UnEUaFdrPEjj) and covered PRs #11353-#11640. Checked against the live open-PR list: ZERO of 57 name a PR that is still open. Every one had closed. Meanwhile 81 PRs landed on main on 2026-09-17 alone and this file recorded NONE of them. !! THE FINDING IS NOT THAT A MANAGER FORGOT -- IT IS THAT R8 CANNOT TELL. check_manager_scope.py R8 asserts exactly one thing, len(rebasing) > 1, with no freshness check of any kind, so a file whose every entry died a week ago passes it TRIVIALLY and by VACUITY. R8 is the only mechanical enforcement of the manager's merge-queue base duty, and it is satisfied by an empty-of-live-work file. !! THAT IS THE SAME SHAPE THIS FILE'S OWN _doc DESCRIBES BEING FIXED: R8 exists because the queue was once cited as 'the state of record' and found on no branch and in no commit. The remedy made the FILE exist. It did not make the file TRUE, and a dead file passes the guard exactly as a live one does -- the failure moved one hop rather than closing. !! DO NOT READ THE REPLACED ENTRIES AS A REBUILT QUEUE. This manager did NOT re-enter the ~60 open PRs it has not assessed; inventing entries for work it never scheduled would manufacture a record, which is the harm the work store's README already names (a false edge is worse than a missing one). What is here is only the four PRs this manager actually drove on 2026-09-17. The other ~77 that landed today did so through their own lanes' auto-merge and never passed through this file, which is itself worth knowing about what this file does and does not cover.
